account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arrived from Sao Paulo. He presented a French passport at primary inspection. A release from U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) states that the officer used the facial comparison biometric technology, which confirmed that the man was not a match to the passport. In secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News that the man was apprehended, processed and returned to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology. CBP releases record a second (8 September 2018) and third (1 October 2018) impostor at Dulles. The sources do not name the matching-algorithm vendor. In a September 2020 audit, the U.S. Government Accountability Office reported that CBP officials said that air entry facial recognition had helped identify seven impostors by December 2019. Gizmodo reported on 11 February 2021 that CBP's annual report for fiscal year 2020 showed no impostor flagged at any airport that year, while CBP scanned over 23 million travelers at entry, exit and Preclearance points. Gizmodo also reported that CBP facial recognition detected fewer than 100 impostors at pedestrian crossings that year. A CBP release of 24 September 2021 reports that facial biometrics had stopped, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally since September 2018.

ai_role.statement: The facial comparison match (less than two seconds per CBP) produced the mismatch that triggered secondary inspection. The search and removal were human actions. The documentation is CBP's own release (deployer, not developer) plus NBC with a named CBP official. The algorithm vendor and the match threshold are not in the sources. CBP's “99% match rate” claim is unaudited here.

value.text: A facial mismatch prompted secondary inspection, where officers found a Congolese identity document and then processed the traveler for return to Brazil.

purpose: Verify arriving international travelers' identities by comparing a live photo with passport or visa photos in government holdings, to detect impostors and expedite entry.

ratings.reason: An attempt to enter the United States on another person's genuine passport was stopped and the traveler removed. Sources document no further threat beyond the document fraud.

CBP gained a verified first detection for a system then three days into use at Dulles, and its later releases report repeated catches. Gizmodo reported that CBP's annual report for fiscal year 2020 showed no impostor flagged at any airport that year.

summary: CBP's new facial comparison system at Dulles reported a mismatch for a man presenting a French passport on 22 August 2018; a Congolese ID was found in his shoe and he was returned to Brazil.
